missionCards.name: Wildfire Watch
missionCards.objective: Detect wildfires early from space over a target region.
missionCards.whyItMatters: Early detection gives firefighters hours instead of days. A satellite can watch remote forests that no lookout tower or patrol covers.
missionCards.destinationText: Low Earth orbit (LEO). You choose the orbit type and altitude.

requirements.title: Daily revisit
requirements.text: See the target region at least once per day.
requirements.failText: The satellite does not pass over the region every day. Pick a wider-angle instrument or a higher orbit so each pass covers a wider strip.

requirements.title: Daylight fire detection
requirements.text: Carry an instrument able to detect active fires in daylight.
requirements.failText: None of the chosen instruments can spot an active fire. A shortwave or thermal infrared instrument can, because fires are very bright at those wavelengths.

requirements.title: Enough data on the ground
requirements.text: Downlink at least 1 GB of data per day.
requirements.failText: Too little data reaches the ground each day. Add a ground station for more contact time, or a faster radio.

requirements.title: One year in orbit
requirements.failText: The orbit decays too fast and the satellite re-enters the atmosphere too early. Fly higher, or carry propulsion to raise the orbit.

bonusObjectives.name: Night detection
bonusObjectives.text: Carry a thermal infrared instrument, so fires are also seen at night.

bonusObjectives.name: Twice-daily revisit
bonusObjectives.text: See the region at least twice per day.

bonusObjectives.name: Fast alerts
bonusObjectives.text: Deliver data to the ground within 1 hour of an observation. This needs more ground station contacts.

tradeOffs: Power vs data: a better camera needs more power and produces more data, but ground contact time is short.
Revisit vs sharpness: with one satellite, a daily revisit needs a wide swath (a wide-angle instrument or a higher orbit), and both give less sharp images.
Altitude: a lower orbit gives sharper images but decays sooner.
Orbit type: a sun-synchronous orbit passes at the same local time every day; other orbits may revisit the region more often.
Launch choice: a rideshare is cheap but its orbit is fixed; a dedicated small launcher lets you choose the orbit but takes a large share of the budget.
Technology vs time: advanced parts improve performance but risk missing the fire-season deadline.

sources.note: Starting values for balancing; not real-world figures.
A fire-prone region at mid-latitude, so orbit type matters for revisit and ground contact.

missionCards.name: Lunar Ice Hunter
missionCards.objective: Map water ice in the permanently shadowed craters at the Moon's poles.
missionCards.whyItMatters: Ice at the poles could give future crews water, oxygen and rocket fuel. It also records the history of water in the inner Solar System.
missionCards.destinationText: Low polar lunar orbit, 384,000 km from Earth. You choose the altitude, 50 to 200 km above the surface.

locked.reason: A 6U CubeSat has no room for an ice-detecting instrument together with the propulsion and fuel needed to stop at the Moon.
Without propulsion the spacecraft flies past the Moon. It must fire a thruster to brake into lunar orbit.

requirements.title: Polar lunar orbit
requirements.text: Reach a polar orbit around the Moon (inclination at least 85°).
requirements.failText: The orbit does not pass over the poles, so the shadowed craters are never seen. Aim the insertion burn for a polar orbit.

requirements.title: Ice detection
requirements.text: Carry an instrument able to detect water ice.
requirements.failText: None of the chosen instruments can find ice. A neutron spectrometer, a shortwave infrared spectrometer or a small radar can.

requirements.title: Enough data on Earth
requirements.text: Send at least 0.2 GB of data per day to Earth.
requirements.failText: Too little data reaches Earth. At the Moon's distance radios are much slower; pick an S-band or faster radio, or add deep-space stations.

requirements.title: One year at the Moon
requirements.text: Operate for at least 1 year in lunar orbit.
requirements.failText: The fuel for keeping the orbit runs out before a year. The Moon's lumpy gravity pulls low orbits down; carry more fuel or fly higher.

requirements.title: Enough delta-v
requirements.text: Carry enough delta-v for lunar orbit insertion and one year of station-keeping.
requirements.failText: The spacecraft cannot brake into lunar orbit and keep it for a year. Pick a thruster with a higher specific impulse, carry more fuel, or make the spacecraft lighter.

bonusObjectives.name: Second ice method
bonusObjectives.text: Carry a second, different kind of ice-detecting instrument, so each finding can be checked.

bonusObjectives.name: Low orbit
bonusObjectives.text: Fly at or below 100 km for sharper maps. This needs more fuel.

bonusObjectives.name: Next-day data
bonusObjectives.text: Deliver data to Earth within 24 hours of each pass.

tradeOffs: Fuel vs mass: more fuel means more delta-v, but the extra mass needs a bigger rocket and more fuel again (the rocket equation).
Altitude: a lower orbit gives sharper ice maps but costs more fuel to keep.
Rideshare vs dedicated launch: the lunar rideshare is cheap but small and flies on a fixed date.
Radio vs distance: at 384,000 km every radio is much slower, so a faster radio or more deep-space contact time is needed.
Power: a low lunar orbit spends up to 40% of each orbit in shadow, so the battery must carry the instruments through the dark.

sources.note: Starting values for balancing; not real-world figures.

sources.source: Rough textbook values for small lunar orbiters (no research for this version)
sources.note: Trans-lunar capacity about 0.3 × low-Earth-orbit capacity; insertion about 0.8 km/s; station-keeping 0.05–0.15 km/s per year. Plausible estimates for balancing; distanceKm is the mean Earth–Moon distance.
The south polar region, where the largest permanently shadowed craters are.
